example.title: Finding the Domain of a Transformed Radical Function With an Odd Index

question.explanation:
The domain of $y = \sqrt[4]{x}$ is \[ x \ge 0. \]

To find the domain of $q(x) = 2\sqrt[4]{x+3} - 2,$ we replace $x$ with $x+3$ in the above inequality. This gives \[ {x+3} \ge 0. \]

Solving this inequality, we get

\begin{align} x+3 &\ge 0 \\[3pt] x &\ge -3 \end{align}

Therefore, the domain of $y = q(x)$ is $x \in [-3, \infty).$

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=q(x)$ is shown below.

example.title: Finding the Domain of a Transformed Radical Function With an Even Index

question.explanation:
The domain of $y = \sqrt[6]{x}$ is \[ x \ge 0. \]

To find the domain of $s(x) = \sqrt[6]{2x-4}+1,$ we replace $x$ with $2x-4$ in the above inequality. This gives \[ {2x-4} \ge 0. \]

Solving this inequality, we get

\begin{align} 2x-4 &\ge 0 \\[3pt] 2x &\ge 4\\[3pt] x &\ge 2 \end{align}

Therefore, the domain of $y = s(x)$ is $x \in [2, \infty).$

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=s(x)$ is shown below.
